Madam President, Executive Secretary, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the Asia Pacific Group and as regional chair India, it is an honor to address the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification. We also acknowledge the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for its leadership as President of COP16, for the Riyadh Action Agenda and the initiatives advanced during its Presidency, and for its continued efforts to build trust and consensus among Parties. Excellencies, we meet at a moment when the world for which this Convention was designed is changing faster than the systems established to protect and restore it. Across Asia and the Pacific, from high mountains to the low-lying islands, from hyper-arid deserts and vast rangelands to forests, agricultural plains and coastal mangrove and marine ecosystems, land and water pressures are intensifying. Desertification, land degradation and drought are converging with climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, sea level rise, saltwater intrusion, and coastal and soil erosion. Sand and dust storms cross borders, food and water insecurity deepen, livelihoods are disrupted, communities are displaced, and development gains are placed at risk. In parts of our region, conflict and war compound our pressures and weaken the capacity of people and institutions to reduce land degradation. These are not separate crises arriving one by one. They demand a convention able to see the challenges as a whole, a convention capable of adapting decisions and turning decisions into results and actions. Above all, they demand that COP17 send a strengthening the convention for a better future. That is the single political task before us. A stronger convention is not one that continually expands its agenda, but one that delivers. Clear in purpose, grounded in science, evidence-based policy solutions and technology, responsive to regional realities, and equipped with adequate capacity and resources. Its success must be measured by reduced land degradation, desertification and drought losses, restored soil and ecosystems and more resilient communities. For the Asia-Pacific Group, continuing the work to develop the post-2030 future strategic framework is therefore the central political issue of COP17. It must learn from implementation and the midterm evaluation of the current UNCCD 2018-2030 strategic framework. close the gap between ambition and delivery and establish practical, measurable and strategic objectives. It should complement the SDGs, the climate and biodiversity agendas and global forest goals without duplicating processes or increasing reporting burdens while preserving flexibility for diverse national circumstances. We thank the Asia-Pacific regional representatives, China, Indonesia and Sri Lanka, for representing our region in the intergovernmental working group, for their participation and valuable contribution to develop the proposed vision and key elements of the post-2030 future strategic framework. The new framework must recognize the conventions, two fundamental pillars, desertification and land degradation and drought. These should be distinct, parallel, and mutually reinforcing top level pillars, each supported by adequate political attention, institutional capacity, and implementation pathways and resources. If drought remains structurally subordinate, the global response will remain inadequate. A stronger drought pillar must shift action from crisis response to proactive risk management through national drought plans, monitoring and early warning systems, vulnerability assessments, preparedness, resilient land and water management, early action, regional cooperation and sustained financing. Madam President, excellencies, distinguished delegates and representatives, It is my great honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the European Union and its 27 member states. We would first like to express our gratitude to the authorities and the people of Mongolia and Ulaanbaatar for hosting the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification and all the great efforts made to organize this conference. Madam President, the theme of this COP, Restoring Land, Restoring Hope, underscores the pressing urgency of taking action to combat desertification, land degradation and drought, recognising that people are at the heart of sustainable land management and play a critical role in preventing, halting and reversing land degradation through their knowledge, stewardship and both individual and collective action. The EU and its member states would like to highlight the opportunity presented by the triple COP semester with the COPs of the Convention on Biological Diversity and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, as well as the UN Water Conference, all taking place later this year. It is our common interest that these and other multilateral environmental agreements, without neglecting their specifics, mutually support each other. Measures, plans and practices that target these challenges simultaneously offer an opportunity to improve policy coherence. This synergistic approach is a necessary step to addressing in an effective, efficient and mutually reinforcing way the intersecting environmental crises facing the global community while avoiding competition or duplication between efforts. We welcome the opportunity at COP17 to discuss the progress made by the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Future Strategic Framework and its final report. It is vital that the convention is equipped with a framework that supports effective delivery of its objectives by parties and other institutions after 2030. Finance is one part of this, and as the Global Land Outlook concludes, redirecting finance matters as much as increasing finance. We should therefore address both the future financing of the convention and the progressive elimination, phasing out or repurposing of environmentally harmful subsidies contributing to DLDD. We will work with the conviction that COP17 will draw significant attention from the global community to the growing challenge of drought. Drought risks are globally widespread, exacerbated by climate change, deforestation, and unsustainable land and water management practices, affecting particularly the most vulnerable members of our societies. We look forward to the outcomes of discussions at this COP, particularly on addressing the underlying systemic drivers of drought, enhancing societal and ecosystem resilience, and by fostering the proactive management of drought's impacts. We expect that this COP will strengthen the focus on thematic issues relating to the enabling environment for sustainable land and drought management. This includes securing land tenure, access and rights to land and water for all, strengthening gender responsiveness and equality to advance the implementation of the Gender Action Plan, and to achieve the empowerment of all women and girls, and addressing the root causes of migration and forced displacements driven by DLDD. We also welcome the focus brought by COP17 on the special vulnerabilities of indigenous peoples and local communities, rangelands and pastoralist communities. The UNCCD programmes and actions should further integrate comprehensive and cross-cutting solutions. We need to foster a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to ensure the effective implementation of the Convention. It is essential to strengthen partnerships and engage a diverse array of stakeholders including the private sector, civil society organizations, children and youth, pastoralists, indigenous peoples, local communities, women and girls, persons with disabilities and disadvantaged groups across all levels from community and local to regional, national and global scales, while also valorizing local and traditional knowledge. As we address the urgent challenges of DLDD, it is essential to highlight the EU's commitment to promote, support and adopt transformative action in land management. The impacts of DLDD are increasingly experienced across the territory of the EU. At the same time, the EU and its member states are and will remain a major donor of official development aid to address DLDD. By striving for land degradation neutrality by 2030, we aim to restore ecosystems, enhance food and water security, and support the livelihoods of people, particularly for those in vulnerable situations, including through adopting nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches. This effort requires ownership, innovative and local approaches, building on the experience in the field, and based where appropriate on the implementation of the agroecology practices and principles.
